Title: Spotlight: efficient automated global optimization in rietveld analysis of diffraction data
Text:
Spotlight: efficient automated 
global optimization in rietveld 
analysis of diffraction data
C. M. Biwer1, Z. Feng2,3, D. Finstad4, M. McDonnell5, M. Knezevic2, M. McKerns6,7, 
D. J. Savage3 & S. C. Vogel3
Performing reliable Rietveld analysis on tens or hundreds of powder diffraction datasets from 
parametric or time-resolved experiments often poses a bottleneck in extracting meaningful results 
from the data. While automated analysis of data has recently been demonstrated, high temperature 
annealing studies, during which phase transformations occur and lattice parameters may change due 
to repartitioning of elements, are prime examples where automation by a simple phase identification 
from a database of room temperature structures or automation by sequential refinements is likely to 
fail. To enable reliable, efficient, automated Rietveld analysis, we present a Python package named 
Spotlight, building on established Rietveld packages such as MAUD, GSAS, or GSAS-II, which extends 
the refinement of best fit parameters to a global optimization using an ensemble of optimizers 
leveraging hierarchical parallel execution on high-performance computing clusters. Spotlight further 
enables the efficient design of refinement plans through the iterative automated machine-learning 
of a surrogate for the refinement on which the global optimizations are performed until results from 
the surrogate converge to the response surface data. We demonstrate Spotlight with the analysis 
of uranium molybdenum and Ti–6Al–4V datasets, as well as in two open-source tutorials analyzing 
aluminium oxide and lead sulphate.
Rietveld analysis1,2 is the standard data analysis method to extract crystallographic (eg. lattice parameters, 
atomic displacement parameters, and atomic positions) and micro-structural (eg. volume fractions, texture, 
and dislocation densities) properties from diffraction datasets. Typically, Rietveld analyses use a least-squares 
approach to minimize the discrepancy between the observed intensity and modeled intensity in order to 
determine the set of physical parameters (eg. lattice parameters and volume fractions) that best describes the 
experimental data. To illustrate the method, Fig. 1 shows a powder diffraction pattern characterized by reflections 
(ie. peaks in intensity) for both experimentally observed and modeled intensities. The intensity, width, and 
position of these reflections encode the desired crystallographic and micro-structural properties of a material 
in a diffraction pattern. However, in Rietveld analysis for many parameters it is critical to begin with starting 
values for the least-squares fit that are close to the final values. For example deviations of less than 1% in the 
lattice parameters from the true value can prevent convergence of the analysis as peaks of the measurement and 
model do not overlap. The higher the resolution of a given instrument, the more crucial it is to provide starting 
values for the lattice parameter close to the final value. While for a known phase automated indexing routines 
can provide starting values for lattice parameters of a single phase, for a mixture of phases with substantial 
peak overlap, this approach is not feasible. Finding starting parameters that will converge to a solution and 
the proper identification of the phases is the rate-limiting step in Rietveld analysis since these are determined 
manually, greatly relying on the experience of the analyst and often the result of extensive trial-and-error. The 
requirement of appropriate starting values also leads to the term ‘Rietveld refinement’ rather than ‘Rietveld fit’ 
as by definition the Rietveld analysis refines a provided structural model, including eg. the lattice parameters, 
against the experimental diffraction data.
Due to the sheer amount of data and number of parameters in Rietveld analyses, some software packages 
provide simple automation from a template refinement or using the previous parameter set as starting values

(so-called sequential refinement), but without allowing to program parameter variation sequences or conditional 
refinements. Examples include seqgsas in GSAS3, batch mode in MAUD4,5, sequential analyses in GSAS-II6 or 
SrRietveld7. The gsaslanguage8 scripting language for GSAS and MILK9 (MAUD Interface Language Kit) for 
MAUD provide more flexibility by scripting the entire refinement including conditional refinements based eg. 
on the weight fraction of a phase. However, automation of the Rietveld analysis does not solve the problem 
of finding starting values in the refinement for crucial parameters such as the lattice parameters that lead to 
convergence or identification of phases present in a given dataset. This is a significant burden on the analyst. 
Therefore, a tool that successfully identifies the crystallographic phases present and predicts their proper initial 
lattice parameters for a subsequent refinement script could accelerate the development of refinement plans and 
delivery of scientific insight from experiments.
However, applying a serial, brute-force approach like most software currently offers to a dataset with several 
phases and a realistic lattice parameter range for each phase would be computationally expensive. Even a single 
refinement may take tens of seconds to complete depending on its complexity, eg. the number of phases or 
number of histograms involved. The time-to-completion could be days or weeks on single user’s machine 
typically used for Rietveld analysis. Therefore, automating the evaluation of many choices of initial values and 
phase combinations in parallel would accelerate the trial-and-error attempts made by the analyst. Additionally, 
using machine-learning to produce an accurate surrogate for the refinements could significantly reduce the 
time-to-solution (as in Fig. 2).
In this paper, we present a software package called Spotlight to address these issues. Spotlight leverages 
machine-learning and ensembles of fast local optimizers executed in parallel on heterogenous computing

resources (from clusters to single machines) to faciliate the efficient discovery of starting values for Rietveld 
refinements that produce globally optimal refinement results.  In particular, we focus on using Spotlight to find 
a subset of parameters, such as initial lattice parameters and phase fractions, as starting points for Rietveld 
refinements. The ‘full refinement’ uses the values from Spotlight as starting values and refines incrementally the 
full parameter set. Spotlight replaces the selecting, or guessing, of starting values by a human with a machine. 
Hence, Spotlight is complementary to other packages with Rietveld analysis methods and their scripting tools. 
This approach is fundamentally different from the automation approaches available with existing packages 
where the analyst must manually change the parameter values and rerun the script for a batch or serial 
refinement. Some other previous work has been done to demonstrate how the computational speed is improved 
using parallelization in crystallographic functions10; however, this accelerates the crystal structure solution and 
does not address the purpose of this package that uses parallelism to determine initial values and optimize the 
design of refinement plans for parametric studies, ie. crystal or microstructural changes as a function of eg. time, 
temperature, pressure, applied load, magnetic field, etc. This previous work is complementary to Spotlight which 
has a plug-and-play design to use other software and configurations.
Other previous work has applied BBO-Rietveld11,12 which uses a hyperparameter optimization to perform 
global optimization in the Rietveld refinement parameter space. Spotlight and BBO-Rietveld differ in both their 
methodology and the scalability of parallelization across compute resources. The implementation of BBO-
Rietveld12 uses the hyperparameter framework Optuna13,14 to directly probe the Rietveld parameter space for 
global optimization, while Spotlight constructs a surrogate model by probing the Rietveld parameter space 
with optimization algorithms. The trained surrogate model is continuously updated and can be utilized in 
real time. O’Leary et al.15 gives a more extensive discussion on the differences between Bayesian Optimization

Results
Spotlight has been developed to efficiently learn and accurately predict the response of an expensive function 
by using an ensemble of optimizers to provide a feedback-driven search for the local extrema of the response 
surface. An example is shown in Fig. 2 using an ensemble of local optimizers to learn the R-factor19 surface for 
a single dataset collected for a titanium alloy by varying the lattice parameters a and c of α-Ti. Here, a sampling 
of the parameter space is drawn, and a local optimization algorithm is executed at each sampled point (a, c) 
to find the nearest local minima or maxima of the R-factor surface. The values of the surface are recorded in a 
central database as the local optimizations transverses the surface. A surrogate for the true R-factor response 
surface is then learned by training a machine-learning algorithm on the sampled data. In Fig. 2, we depict the 
learning of an accurate R-factor surrogate, where the surface is a function of inputs a and c. As more points 
are evaluated, and thus more refinements are performed, the resolution and accuracy of the R-factor surrogate 
improves. As more extrema of the R-factor surface are discovered, the difference between the predicted values 
from the surrogate and truth (ie. the refinement results) decreases. As the difference between the surrogate and 
truth tends toward zero, the global minimum of the surrogate becomes predictive of the best-fit parameters to 
use as the starting values for the full refinement. The efficiency with which this happens depends on the choice 
of sampling algorithm, optimization algorithm, and termination conditions. We describe these plug-and-play 
choices in “Methods” section.
Spotlight contains a command-line executable, called spotlight_minimize, that implements 
this methodology for the user. It launches a number of subprocesses, typically one subprocess per CPU, as 
illustrated in Fig. 3. Each subprocess in Fig. 3 executes the local optimization in Fig. 3 to minimize a refinement. 
Subprocesses are parallel-distributed using mpi4py which provides bindings for the Message Passing Interface 
(MPI) standard for Python16–18. MPI allows us to parallelize over multiple machines in distributed-computing 
networks, instead of parallelizing only on a single machine using Python built-in multiprocesing modules. At 
the start of the subprocess, a set of parameters (eg. lattice parameters) is drawn from the parameter space. Next, 
a local optimization algorithm is initiated at the drawn point in the parameter space; if a global optimization 
algorithm has been selected then a member of the population is initialized. The local optimization algorithm 
minimizes the analyst’s function that uses GSAS or MAUD to return the the R-factor value. After each internal 
iteration in the optimization algorithm, called a generation, a termination condition for the algorithm is checked; 
this is the blue-colored decision box in Fig. 3. If it fails, then the local optimization algorithm repeats for another 
generation. If it passes, then another termination condition for the subprocess is checked. If the termination 
condition for the subprocess is not satisfied, then the loop restarts. The results are written to a database20 shared 
by all subprocesses and capable of parallel read and write; therefore, all subprocesses have access to its contents. 
This allows previous information to be used by new or existing subprocesses to more effectively select their 
initial values. At the end, the global minimum contains the lattice parameters, phase fractions, etc. to use for the 
full refinement.
Spotlight is distributed with two tutorials21,22 meant to demonstrate how to use Spotlight to determine the 
initial parameters for a dataset. We refer users to the Spotlight documentation for the current instructions on 
running these tutorials at https://github.com/lanl/spotlight. In this section, we briefly describe the two tutorials 
and their expected results. We also demonstrate Spotlight on case studies of uranium molybdenum and titanium 
alloys to suggest initial lattice parameters using both GSAS and MILK in practice.
Aluminium oxide
The first tutorial analyzes a X-ray diffraction dataset of aluminium oxide21 using GSAS. The analysis is discussed 
in detail in the GSAS manual and we reproduced it in a scripted analysis using gsaslanguage. The Spotlight 
tutorial is meant to emphasize that Spotlight is flexible to which variables can be optimized in the trial refinement 
– it is not limited to only lattice parameters and phase fractions, but may be applied for other parameters such

as atom positions and anisotropic atomic displacement. For demonstrative purposes, we include 23 parameters 
in the trial refinement using Spotlight where each parameter is bounded ±5% from the results of the scripted 
analysis. The suggested initial lattice parameters by Spotlight are in Table 1. We use the Darwin cluster at Los 
Alamos National Laboratory which is a large, heterogeneous cluster composed of over 350 nodes with varying 
architectures. We only use nodes with Intel Xeon E5-2660V3 (Haswell) CPUs where each node is capable of 
40 subprocesses. 160 subprocessors were executed across four nodes on the Darwin cluster for 2 hours (ie. one 
allocation), and we inspect the results after 2 hours.
Running the tutorial, 285 local optimizations were initialized which evaluated 685065 diffraction patterns. 
Since it takes ∼1 s to evaluate one diffraction pattern, then the same number of evaluations executed in serial 
would take >7.9 days. The final χ2(⃗x) value from the Spotlight optimization search was 2.250, compared to 1.918 
in the scripted analysis. Again, the purpose is not to get an exact match but rather acceptable starting parameters 
within 1% to ensure convergence of the full refinement. We repeat the tutorial with four unique random seeds 
and we report those results in Table 1. The tutorial is designed to show consistency in predicting suitable starting 
values using all 23 parameters, but for brevity we only show the lattice parameters at the top of Table 1 which are 
within ≲0.1% of the scripted values.
Lead sulphate
The second tutorial analyzes a X-ray diffraction dataset of lead sulphate22. This tutorial uses a GSAS-II refinement 
and optimizes the input lattice parameters of the orthorhombic PbSO4 phase. The lattice parameter found using 
a scripted GSAS-II analysis are a = 8.474 Å, b = 5.394 Å, and c = 6.954 Å. The purpose of this tutorial is to 
emphasize the plug-and-play nature of Spotlight. We can alter the termination condition of the optimizers, where 
each local optimization is terminated once more than 25 diffraction patterns were evaluated. This termination 
was chosen to evaluate at minimum as many diffraction patterns as the expected value which is 1000 samples. 
We drew the initial positions of the local optimizations from the 3-dimensional uniform distribution bounded 
by a in 8.474 ± 10% Å, b in 5.394 ± 10% Å, and c in 6.954 ± 10% Å. We used a single Darwin node and 1632 
diffraction patterns were evaluated before its allocation ended after 2 hours. This is higher than 1000 samples 
because we allowed each optimizer to complete its current generation after passing 1000 samples. The best-fit 
lattice parameters recovered using Spotlight were: a = 8.472 Å, b = 5.399 Å, and c = 6.945 Å. These values 
agree with the scripted analysis using GSAS-II to within ≲ 0.1%, thus ensuring convergence of the subsequent 
full Rietveld fit. We note that identifying suitable starting values for non-cubic systems, in particular with larger 
unit cells, is particularly difficult by trial-and-error methods due to severe peak overlap.
Uranium molybdenum alloy
Four datasets of uranium 10%-wt. molybdenum samples were characterized for its annealing behavior between 
420 °C and 520 °C with the High-Pressure Preferred Orientation (HIPPO)24 instrument at the Los Alamos 
Neutron Science Center (LANSCE), a pulsed neutron spallation source. The datasets collected with HIPPO 
consists of 12003He detector tubes arranged on 45 detector panels on five rings around the incident beam. Each 
ring is integrated resulting in five histograms per run; however, only two rings (144.4° and 90°) are used in this 
analysis. The diffraction pattern of the 90° ring from data at room temperature is shown in Fig. 1.
We demonstrate how Spotlight has been applied to the 490 °C dataset, which consists of 117 10-minute 
integrated runs, to hierarchically design a refinement plan using Spotlight. This consists of two steps: (i) select 
a subset of six ‘anchor runs’ and use Spotlight to suggest initial lattice parameters and phase fractions, and then 
(ii) use the suggested initial lattice parameters and phase fractions to design a gsaslanguage script that uses the 
anchor runs results to initialize nearby runs. These results are compared to a reference refinement that was 
designed manually with only gsaslanguage.
The first step in our hierarchical design of a refinement is to select a set of anchor runs and run a trial 
refinement using Spotlight on each. The 420 °C dataset consists of 117 runs, and an anchor runs was chosen 
every 20-th run; there are six anchor runs in total. The trial refinement for each anchor run was designed using 
the following settings with Spotlight. The structural model included the cubic γ-U, orthorhombic α-U, cubic γ1

969512, 687318, 684039, 818511, 665697, and 681987 diffraction patterns respectively. A single diffraction

The results of the trial refinement for the six anchor runs are shown in Figs. 4 and 5. The nearest anchor 
run’s results were used to set the initial lattice parameters and phase fractions for each run in a gsaslanguage 
script. In Fig.  4, we present the lattice parameter for the γ-U phase throughout the 117 runs. The phase 
fractions of the trial refinement for the six anchor runs are shown in Fig. 5. We compare the results from the 
refinement hierarchically-designed using Spotlight versus a refinement using only gsaslanguage. In Fig. 5, we 
see a discrepancy between the two results. γ-U is meta-stable and should decompose into α-U and γ1-U when 
heated. We expect the weight fraction to begin at 0 %-wt and apply a constraint that γ1-U must go to 0 %-wt. 
and explore a degeneracy between the γ-U and the α-U and γ1-U phases. We were able to identify the solutions 
with 0%-wt. for γ1-U and its impact on γ-U and α-U. Without this tool, we would have to perform a number 
of trial-and-error refinements trying to explore where the solutions with 0%-wt. γ1-U exist. A crystallographic 
interpretation is beyond the scope of this paper and a discussion will be included in a future publication. The 
previously-unanalyzed 420 °C, 460 °C and 520 °C datasets were analyzed using this same methodology.
Titanium alloy
The following is an example analysis of a laser powder bed fusion Ti–6Al–4V sample encased in a 316L steel 
container. We analyzed a set of X-ray diffraction data collected from the Forming and Shaping Technology 
(FAST) beamline at the Cornell High-Energy Synchrotron Source (CHESS)25. The sample was heated in situ 
from 17 to 1050 °C at a nominal rate of 1.6 °C per second, followed by a solutionizing hold, a quench to 800 °C, 
a hold to observe transformation behavior of β-Ti, and cooling to ambient. The 2-D diffraction was collected in 
a burst mode; bursts were summed and caked using pyFAI26, resulting in 437 1-D histograms.
We first determined the possible ranges of the lattice parameters for the α-Ti, β-Ti, and steel phases by 
manually analyzing the 200oC histogram towards the end of the time series using MAUD and examining the 
half-width shifts of the peaks to find the set of target lattice parameters as initial guesses. The initial targets are 
set as: α-Ti a = 2.931 Å, α-Ti c = 4.678 Å, β-Ti = 3.233 Å, and steel a = 3.599 Å. The lower and upper bounds 
were set to 0.0125 Å below and 0.075 Å above the targets, respectively, based on thermal expansion. For example, 
we assume steel’s coefficient of thermal expansion to be 15×10-6 °C-1 and with a 1033  °C temperature increase 
the lattice parameter would increase by 0.054 Å. The actual bounds are set to be slightly larger than the expected 
range for flexibility and cover edge cases. We then binned the bounded ranges by 4, 4, 7, and 3 bins respectively. 
The β-Ti phase has finer bins due to the peaks overlapping with the other two phases. The number of bins is 
chosen to sufficiently discretize the expected parameter ranges based on thermal expansion, where for the steel 
phase each bin would span a change of 0.0292 Å, corresponding to about 540 °C of temperature change. The bins 
are used to define a mesh grid of 336 points with all possible combinations of the lattice parameters.

We use MILK to refine the background and overall intensity parameters while setting up the folders for batch 
processing. Next, we performed Rietveld analyses for each histogram in the dataset with every set of lattice 
parameter in the 336-point grid, totaling 146832 Rietveld refinements over the 437 diffraction histograms. It 
was immediately apparent that the R-factor value Rwp was not sufficient as the sole criterion for determining 
the best result that is also physically meaningful. This condition occurs when model deficiencies are present 
(e.g. inappropriate background) and peak overlaps are present. For example, when fitting a histogram that 
should have zero β-Ti phase fraction, the fit that predicted a zero β-Ti phase fraction has a higher Rwp than 
a fit that predicts some small amount of β-Ti fraction, causing the grid optimization to select the latter as the 
better result. The inclusion of β-Ti was found to improve the background fit. To address this, we increased the 
number of bins for β-Ti, adjusted the harmonic texture to have a higher degree of freedom, increased the back 
polynomial degree, and implemented algorithms to check the results and re-evaluate the fits when the selected 
best-fit parameters, such as crystallite size and microstrain, are not physical.
The Rietveld analyses are wrapped inside the cost function where MAUD refinements are called and the Rwp 
factor is extracted and returned as the error to be minimized. For the quality of the data, 4% phase fraction is the 
minimum phase fraction that can routinely be refined, so any phase fraction below 4% during the refinement 
is set to 0% automatically. The refined phase fractions, temperature, and lattice parameter evolution over time 
are shown in Fig. 6. On a Mac Studio computer with the Apple M1 Ultra chip, 128 GB of memory and using 15 
parallel processes, on average, each histogram took 2.3 minutes to complete, each refinement procedure took 
about 6.2 seconds, and the overall process completed in about 17 hours.
Also plotted are the error bars for each histogram refinement, visualized as shaded regions above and below 
the respective curves. The top figure in Fig. 6 plots the phase fractions on the left y-axis and the temperature on 
the right y-axis. As the temperature increases, β-Ti phase develops volume fraction above around 800 °C. At 
1050 °C, the sample completely transforms to β-Ti and the α-Ti phase fraction is zero. After the quenching to 
800 °C at 1200 seconds, α-Ti phase continues to grow over the temperature hold period. During cool down, the 
phase fractions reach steady state with α-Ti phase at about 75% and β-Ti phase at about 25%. The bottom figure 
in Fig. 6 plots the evolution of lattice parameters, shown as lattice strains for α-Ti, β-Ti, and steel phases. The 
overall trend follow the temperature curve as expected. Where the phase fraction is zero, the lattice parameters 
cannot be reliably refined and the lattice parameters of the phase are not shown.
Discussion
In this paper, we outline Spotlight which parallelizes trial refinement plans to find initial starting values for 
parameters in Rietveld refinements. In particular, we focus on lattice parameters and phase fractions. However, 
the plug-and-play design can robustly be used with other software (eg. GSAS, GSAS-II, and MAUD), as well as 
additional applications such as refining crystal structure by searching structural units, bond angles and lengths, 
and other constraints. The source code, tutorials, and documentation of Spotlight are available for download 
from https://github.com/lanl/spotlight.

We would like to emphasize that Spotlight is a tool that was designed to provide reliable starting values for 
Rietveld analysis, and it is not immune to the challenges commonly encountered in standard Rietveld analysis. 
As mentioned in “Introduction” section, phase identification is a rate limiting step in Rietveld analysis. For 
instance, if an unknown phase is present in the sample, then an expert is still needed. However, if we can frame 
these issues as an optimization problem, then tools like Spotlight can be used. In this case, Spotlight can include 
categorical variables such as on-off bits for each phase in a collection. This enables the analyst to explore a range 
of phase combinations. Spotlight can be utilized for these types of optimization problems that assist the expert.
Methods
In this section, we describe configurable choices in Spotlight’s plug-and-play design for using an optimization 
search to find inputs for refinements using distributed-computing resources. There are several choices to consider 
such as: how to define a cost function to optimize, when to terminate all subprocess doing trial refinements and 
start the full refinement, where to place new optimizers in the parameter space, what optimization algorithm to 
use, and when to terminate the optimization algorithm.
Defining a cost function
The user must define a cost function for the trial refinements which given inputs (eg. lattice parameters) returns 
a quantity to be minimize (eg. an R-factor value). In Spotlight the user simply writes a Python function to be

and MILK in the titanium alloy example. To illustrate this, a short example of minimizing an inverted Gaussian

Spotlight cost functions can be used with alternative parallelization frameworks as well. For example, if the user 
wants to run in parallel on their own machine, without access to a high-performance computing cluster or MPI 
implementation, they can design a script with the Plan class and use tools such as pathos20 for parallelization. 
An example is shown in Fig. 7. The titanium alloy example in “Titanium alloy” section was paralleized using 
pathos on a laptop, whereas all other examples in this paper used MPI on high-performance computing clusters.
Choices for sampling the parameter space
Spotlight has the capability to place new optimizers using several different distributions or methods. The examples 
in “Results” section used two methods. The two tutorials and uranium molybdenium alloy example sampled 
new trial points from a uniform distribution. The titantium alloy example started all optimizers at bin centers 
of a lattice. More complex sampling algorithms can take into account exploration using prior knowledge or 
legacy data. For example, Spotlight can select new points that maximize the Euclidean distance from previously 
evaluated points to explore new regions.
Choices for surrogate-assisted optimization
We described the sampling of the parameter space which is written to a database. An example is shown in Fig. 2, 
where the top row shows a database of sampled points (a, c) and their response Rwp from executing the Rietveld 
software. We can fit a surrogate model to the sampled points so it approximates the Rwp surface, as shown in 
the bottom of Fig. 2. This surrogate model can then be used in a surrogate-assisted optimization , where the 
surrogate is used to find the global minima of a response surface using fewer cost function evaluations. The 
surrogate model is far less expensive to evaluate than performing the full Rietveld analysis, and thus, we can 
quickly find the minima, maxima, and inflection points of the surrgoate model, and take the global minima of 
the surrogate as the best, approximate value for a and c. The surrogate modeling is implemented in Spotlight and 
can be constructed using RBF interpolation , Gaussian process regression , or artificial neural networks . The 
surrogate model is updated with new points whenever new Rietveld results invalidate the current surrogate.
Choices for optimization algorithms
Spotlight depends on mystic27 which contains a library of constrained optimization alogrithms. There are local 
(eg. Newton’s28, Nelder-Mead29, and Powell’s methods30) and global (eg. differential evolution) optimization 
algorithms that can be used to minimize the test refinement. Each optimization may have constraints added. For 
the examples within this paper, we use the implementation of Powell’s methods30 in mystic which is based on the 
SciPy31 implementation. One motivation for using Powell’s method in our examples is that it does not require a 
smooth, differentiable function.

Choices for termination conditions of the optimizations
The optimization algorithm in “Choices for optimization algorithms” section will iterate until a termination condition 
is met. There are several termination conditions that can be selected for the optimization algorithms; such as 
termination after a certain number of evaluations, number of generations (ie. steps) of the local optimization, or if a 
threshold is pass in the differential change between generations. In the “Results” section examples, we terminated once 
the normalized differential change for the i-th generation’s χ2(⃗x) or R-factor below a threshold ξ is

for optimization algorithms” section, g is the number of generations to look back for comparison, and ξ is a threshold 
set by the analyst. Once the ratio from Eq. 1 is satisfied, then the optimization terminates.
Choices for termination conditions of the optimization search
In “Results” section we use several different strategies for terminating the optimization search (ie. the yellow-colored 
decision box in Fig. 3): (a) a time limit for the alumina oxide tutorial and uranium molybdenium alloy example, 
(b) a set number of evaluations for the lead sulphate tutorial, and (c) a set number of optimizations for the titanium 
alloy example. Spotlight has been designed to use distributed-computing networks, and typically supercomputing 
facilities set time limits for allocations of computing resources. And for periods of available computing, we run the 
optimization search until the high-performance computing cluster allocation time limit expires and then inspect the 
results. In a worse case scenario, a uniform sampling like this can be shown to have a strong dependence on the total

The tutorials in “Aluminium oxide” and “Lead sulphate” sections restrict the lattice parameter search to 
ranges of ±5% and ±10%, respectively. In practice, variations in lattice parameters due to changes in chemistry 
and/or temperature typically do not exceed 5%. Additionally, phase fractions are inherently constrained within 
the range [0, 1]. Using Eq. 3, along with the time required to compute the cost function, and the number of 
available processors, one can roughly estimate the time to complete the search in a worse-case senario. From 
Eq. 3, extending the search bounds would result in longer computational times.
